video_title: Lawfare Daily: How Terrorist Groups are Using Artificial Intelligence
gist: Field research based on interviews with Boko Haram members (2023 through mid-2025) finds the group uses commercial AI models as a full-cycle operational assistant — weapons identification, tactical planning, IED chemistry and drone weaponization — far beyond the propaganda use cases most analysts track, while systematically defeating guardrails via jailbreak training from ISIS-linked operatives, multi-provider account shopping and task decomposition. A counterpoint from Somalia shows governments currently winning the AI race in counterterrorism (AI camera networks, Somali-language social monitoring), raising an unaddressed second risk: state repression with no vendor or policy guardrails at all.

insights.claim: Interviews with Boko Haram members indicate AI has become an embedded general-purpose technology across the full insurgent cycle — preparing attacks, executing them, and analyzing failures afterward — functioning as a 24/7 operational assistant rather than a propaganda tool.
insights.speaker: Antonia (Cambridge program on AI science and policy)
entities: Cambridge program on AI science and policy
insights.so_what: Reframes terrorist AI risk from content moderation to operational capability uplift; misuse-monitoring built only around propaganda detection will miss the dominant use case.
insights.quote: AI has become embedded really as a general purpose technology that can provide information across the full insertion cycle

insights.claim: Boko Haram has changed its battlefield doctrine around AI: captured weapons are now brought back to camp where commanders type in the serial number and model to learn what they have and how to service and troubleshoot it, replacing a slow dependency on ISIS network contacts and in-person trainers.
insights.speaker: Antonia
insights.so_what: A concrete, measurable capability change — removal of a training/latency bottleneck — that is invisible to online-content-based threat monitoring.
insights.quote: Now the new rule is that whatever you get, you bring it back to the camp.

insights.claim: Boko Haram used AI for tactical adaptation against specific counterterrorism measures, including learning to attack with smaller coordinated units and to cross defensive trenches the Nigerian military built around bases and towns using motorcycles — an obstacle that previously stopped them.
insights.speaker: Antonia
insights.so_what: Demonstrates AI closing an adaptation loop against physical fortifications, meaning defensive infrastructure investments depreciate faster than planners assume.

insights.claim: Boko Haram reportedly used AI to improve explosive design — which additional chemicals make IEDs more powerful, and how to defuse unexploded ordnance to extract military-grade explosive and repurpose it — with a commander framing AI as an accuracy substitute for lethal trial-and-error.
insights.speaker: Antonia
insights.so_what: Direct evidence that chem/energetics uplift from commercial models is already happening at the low end, not just in hypothetical CBRN scenarios.
insights.quote: as one commander put it, trial and error can kill you. AI gives you accuracy.

insights.claim: Respondents said AI ultimately supplied the specific answers that let the group master drone weaponization after long experimentation using the open internet and foreign assistance had failed to get them there.
insights.speaker: Antonia
insights.so_what: Shows AI's marginal value is in resolving the last technical blocker, so capability jumps appear suddenly after long plateaus — a poor fit for linear threat forecasting.

insights.claim: Some of the largest claimed gains are inherently unmeasurable from outside: interviewees reported reducing casualties within their own ranks, an effect analysts cannot quantify and which is confounded by many other variables.
insights.speaker: Antonia
insights.so_what: Warns that absence of visible attack-metric change is weak evidence of absence of AI uplift; measurement bias runs toward underestimating the effect.

insights.claim: AI companies pushed back on the Boko Haram findings by arguing safeguards improved after the 2023–mid-2025 study window, but even the latest models remain jailbreakable — from simple techniques like writing prompts as poetry to universal jailbreaks that act as reusable keys succeeding on most harmful requests across an entire domain.
insights.speaker: Antonia
insights.so_what: Vendor claims of improved safety are a moving target that has not closed the exploit class; regulatory pressure on jailbreak resistance is likely to continue.

insights.claim: AI providers are not facing isolated bad users but trained, networked adversaries: Boko Haram members received in-person training from ISIS-linked operatives plus everyday online assistance in prompt engineering and jailbreaking, with techniques shared across the network.
insights.speaker: Antonia
insights.so_what: Implies safety evaluation designed around single-user red-teaming systematically understates real-world attack capability.
insights.quote: these companies don't just face isolated users um but really like trained network and organized adversaries that share the latest ways to to jailbreak models

insights.claim: Groups arbitrage uneven safety enforcement across providers — maintaining multiple accounts on multiple models so that a refusal on one system simply routes the request to a weaker one, and comparing answers across models to find the most useful.
insights.speaker: Antonia
insights.so_what: Safety becomes a lowest-common-denominator problem across the industry, strengthening the case for cross-provider minimum standards rather than per-company policy.

insights.claim: A further evasion method is task decomposition — breaking a harmful request into smaller, harmless-looking pieces that individually pass safety filters and are reassembled by the user.
insights.speaker: Antonia
insights.so_what: Per-prompt classification is structurally insufficient; detection has to operate at the account/session/pattern level.

insights.claim: Initial research shows much lower refusal rates in Somali because it is a low-resource language, meaning advertised guardrails may simply not function outside dominant languages like English — even though the same models still score well on multilingual capability benchmarks.
insights.speaker: Tricia Bacon and Antonia
insights.so_what: Capability generalizes across languages faster than safety does — a measurable, testable gap that mirrors the English-dominant content-moderation failure of the social media era.
insights.quote: there's much lower levels of refusal in Somali in part because it is sort of a low resource language

insights.claim: Boko Haram enforces a rank-based AI access policy — only mid-ranking commanders and above may use the models — consistent with its existing restrictions on internet and phone access, because a group relying on coercion does not trust its foot soldiers with capable tools.
insights.speaker: Antonia
insights.so_what: Internal control policy caps diffusion of AI benefit within a group, so capability gains concentrate at the command layer rather than spreading uniformly.

insights.claim: Boko Haram has built dedicated internal AI units responsible for prompting, jailbreaking, and cascading that knowledge down the hierarchy to train others — mirroring how legitimate organizations stand up centers of excellence for new technology.
insights.speaker: Antonia
insights.so_what: Tracking which groups train whom, and how that expertise spreads, is a concrete intelligence collection target with observable structure.

insights.claim: The group's constraints are more technical than organizational: it hits hallucinations and says it still has to supplement model output with human judgment, and there were incidents where following AI instructions during explosives experimentation killed people.
insights.speaker: Antonia
insights.so_what: Model unreliability is currently an incidental brake on misuse — meaning capability improvements in accuracy translate directly into misuse uplift.

insights.claim: Boko Haram's self-identified main limitation is a shortage of in-house technical expertise, and members are aware they could exploit these models far more effectively if they had it.
insights.speaker: Antonia
insights.so_what: Human capital, not model access, is the binding constraint — so agentic tooling that lowers required operator skill would be the step-change to watch.

themes.theme: Somalia: the state is winning the AI race

insights.claim: In Mogadishu the inverse of the usual story is happening — the government, not the militants, is gaining the AI advantage: city-wide camera networks monitor vehicles, license plates and drivers, suppressing al-Shabaab's vehicle-borne IED attacks, cameras are installed in businesses al-Shabaab extorts, and a Somali-language AI social media monitoring system is about to deploy.
insights.speaker: Tricia Bacon
insights.so_what: Demand for AI surveillance tooling in low-resource-language, low-institutional-capacity states is real and being filled today — a growing market with essentially no external guardrails.

insights.claim: Al-Shabaab's lag is partly explained by an unprecedented and rarely-discussed US air campaign whose pace of strikes suppresses technology use — the group avoids phones and internet to avoid detection — while it simultaneously tries to absorb drone capability learned from the Houthis, and two new technologies at once is hard for any mature organization.
insights.speaker: Tricia Bacon
insights.so_what: Kinetic pressure functions as an indirect AI-adoption brake, but the same pressure may later force innovation — the speaker explicitly declines to bet the lag persists.
insights.quote: I wouldn't bet that that will remain that way.

insights.claim: AI capability acquired by a government for counterterrorism does not stay confined to counterterrorism — social media monitoring and vehicle tracking become tools of broader political repression, and unlike the vendor-versus-terrorist dynamic there is no company positioned to intercede on a state's own in-house monitoring platform.
insights.speaker: Tricia Bacon
insights.so_what: The unpriced governance risk is state-side, in countries with immature political systems — and it is structurally harder to solve than the cat-and-mouse of consumer model guardrails.
insights.quote: when a government is gaining this kind of AI capability for counterterrorism purposes, it doesn't stay counterterrorism purposes

insights.claim: Beyond monitoring, the harder issue is governments using AI systems for targeting with reduced human involvement — a concern already raised about the United States and Israel, and far more dangerous in places with fewer guardrails, since it lets states apply violence systematically without requiring human complicity.
insights.speaker: Tricia Bacon
insights.so_what: Defense-AI targeting policy, not chatbot safety, may become the higher-stakes regulatory battleground — and tech companies currently take almost no public stance on government use limits.

themes.theme: Propaganda is the overrated use case

insights.claim: AI-generated propaganda receives disproportionate attention in AI risk discussions largely because online data is easy to collect, and because AI is misconceived as a smart chatbot — an extension of social media — a comparison that significantly underestimates its capability.
insights.speaker: Antonia
insights.so_what: Availability bias in the research base is skewing policy attention toward the least consequential misuse channel; the operational uses are offline and invisible.
insights.quote: AI is often a bit misconceived as like a very smart chatbot an extension of social media and I think that comparison is a bit flawed um and significantly underestimates AI's capability

insights.claim: Unofficial jihadist media outlets and online supporters adopted AI well before the terrorist groups themselves, and online forums saw controversy with some arguing AI use is prohibited and un-Islamic because models are trained on Western voices and faces — but public reticence may reflect deliberate concealment rather than genuinely slow adoption by the groups.
insights.speaker: Antonia
insights.so_what: Public-facing adoption signals are a biased proxy for real adoption; groups have reasons to hide AI use that supporters do not.

insights.claim: A group's propaganda incentive to adopt AI depends on its strategic aim, not its sophistication: al-Shabaab already runs a well-oiled multilingual machine in Swahili, Somali, Arabic and English and did not need AI to fix what works, whereas Islamic State Khorasan is expansionist and reaches for AI to add new languages and extend its footprint.
insights.speaker: Tricia Bacon
insights.so_what: A usable predictor of which groups adopt AI propaganda first — expansion-seeking groups with unmet language reach, not the most capable ones.

insights.claim: The terrorism analysis field's expertise is mismatched to the problem because it was built on studying social media use, a fundamentally different technology, and because technology fluency skews young while established analysts are less able to grasp the range of changes.
insights.speaker: Daniel Byman (host)
insights.so_what: Explains a persistent blind spot in the threat literature — and argues the analytic gap is generational and institutional, not just informational.
insights.quote: you're not going to see social media used in the same way to you know improve you know bomb design uh by 10%

insights.claim: The realistic near-term picture is incremental, not revolutionary — roughly 5–10%, maybe 20% improvements in scattered spheres among some organizations, not a group going from zero to building a nuclear weapon.
insights.speaker: Tricia Bacon
insights.so_what: A calibrated baseline against the doomsday framing — useful for pricing near-term national-security risk without dismissing tail scenarios.
insights.quote: it's not universal it's 5% 10% % improvements in different spheres among some organizations

insights.claim: The real test of whether AI is revolutionary is not mature organizations with established processes but new organizations born in the AI era that build AI in as a pillar from the start — whether they develop capabilities more quickly and more innovatively is the open question.
insights.speaker: Tricia Bacon
insights.so_what: A specific forward indicator to watch: the founding cohort of post-2023 groups, not the incumbents everyone currently studies.

insights.claim: Compounding efficiency gains and revolution are related rather than opposed: gradual creeping capability can bring a group to an inflection point where it solves a previously blocking technical problem and makes a bigger leap.
insights.speaker: Antonia
insights.so_what: Argues against treating 'incremental' as 'safe' — threshold effects mean linear uplift produces nonlinear outcomes.

insights.claim: Whether AI creates a 'new capability' depends entirely on the reference point — chemical and biological weapons are not new in the abstract but would be new for most terrorist groups — and setting the bar at battlefield novelty sets the threshold for concern far too high.
insights.speaker: Antonia
insights.so_what: A definitional critique with policy teeth: 'no new capabilities' findings in AI evaluations may be measuring against the wrong baseline.
insights.quote: I do worry a bit that we set the bar for what constitutes a new capability or revolution and implicitly also for when we should be worried uh way too high

insights.claim: AI-enabled bioterrorism is more credible than many assume: studies show AI already outperforms human experts on relevant biology tasks and could help design pandemic-capable pathogens, and while building a bioweapon still requires manual lab work, facilities, materials and tools, AI is lowering the technical, operational and motivational barriers that have kept such attacks out of reach.
insights.speaker: Antonia
insights.so_what: Frames uplift as barrier-lowering across three axes including motivation — the motivational channel is rarely modeled in biosecurity evaluations.

insights.claim: The intent side is misjudged: attention focuses on apocalyptic omnicidal cults, but al-Qaeda and ISIS have apocalyptic strains and have tried to build chemical and biological weapons before — their intent has not changed, only the difficulty, so more groups may have incentive to try than assumed.
insights.speaker: Antonia
insights.so_what: Shifts the risk model from rare-actor screening to a much wider intent pool, changing who mitigation should be designed against.

insights.claim: Chemical weapons are currently a more realistic scenario than biological; in the interviews, bio had been discussed at leadership level but seemed out of reach — and notably the contentious part was not acquisition but release.
insights.speaker: Antonia
insights.so_what: A rare interior detail on where the true bottleneck sits, implying acquisition-focused controls may be aimed at the wrong step.

insights.claim: Mitigation should be actor-tiered: a lone individual with limited resources can be disrupted by cutting off access to key materials and information, whereas a well-funded group is a harder target better deterred by raising attack cost and the odds of getting caught.
insights.speaker: Antonia
insights.so_what: A practical segmentation for allocating detection versus denial resources instead of one-size-fits-all controls.

insights.claim: The sharpest way to size the tail risk is counterfactual: what if Aum Shinrikyo, the Unabomber, or al-Qaeda's 1990s camps experimenting with gas had had access to today's AI — actors who already had intent and baseline scientific capability and were not starting from zero.
insights.speaker: Tricia Bacon
insights.so_what: Locates the real danger zone as AI layered on pre-existing scientific capability, not AI creating capability from nothing — a narrower, more tractable screening target.

themes.theme: Policy fixes for industry and government

insights.claim: The core technical ask is cross-provider minimum safety standards so that a refusal from one model does not simply route the user to a weaker competitor — and governments may have to mandate it, since it is unclear whether companies would cooperate to set such standards themselves.
insights.speaker: Antonia
insights.so_what: A specific, checkable regulatory proposal — harmonized refusal floors — that would fall hardest on providers competing on permissiveness.
insights.quote: we need minimum safety standards across providers so that a refusal in one place is not simply an invitation to try another one

insights.claim: Even the most robust safeguards provide very little practical security while highly capable open-weight models are freely available.
insights.speaker: Antonia
insights.so_what: Puts open-weight release policy at the center of the misuse debate — a direct risk factor for firms whose strategy depends on open releases.
insights.quote: the most robust safeguards offer very little practical security if highly capable and open weight models are freely available

insights.claim: Companies should test safeguards against organized, trained adversaries rather than only isolated users, and should stand up an AI threat fusion center combining company and government signals so misuse scattered across platforms is seen as one pattern rather than isolated fragments.
insights.speaker: Antonia
insights.so_what: A concrete institutional design — an ISAC-style body for AI misuse — that would require cross-company data sharing currently absent.
insights.quote: an AI threat fusion center that combines company and government signals

insights.claim: Security agencies and the intelligence community should systematically assess how terrorist groups use AI and trace which groups are being trained by whom and how that expertise spreads, particularly regarding potential WMD development.
insights.speaker: Antonia
insights.so_what: Identifies expertise-diffusion mapping as an under-collected intelligence line with clear observable targets.

insights.claim: The US intelligence community lacks the bureaucratic structure for this: alongside regional and functional focuses it needs people specifically responsible for AI, because the average terrorism analyst cannot keep up with a fast-moving technology while also tracking group operations — and the US is on the cutting edge of using AI in warfare while lacking the analytic and expertise base.
insights.speaker: Tricia Bacon
insights.so_what: A capability-versus-comprehension gap inside the US government — heavy operational adoption without matching analytic tradecraft.

insights.claim: The binding constraint on building government AI expertise is compensation — people with that expertise can make six or seven figures — making hiring and retention an unavoidable and unresolved obstacle for the intelligence community.
insights.speaker: Tricia Bacon
insights.so_what: Private-sector wage pressure structurally caps public-sector AI oversight capacity, a durable asymmetry favoring industry over regulators.
insights.quote: You can make six figures, uh, seven figures with that kind of expertise.
